column1: # The overlay: every place where rhc's Prelude and library modules are to differ from the code the Haskell 2010 Report
# prints, each with its ground (D23 of docs/plans/language/haskell2010.md, the haskell2010 roadmap, as the haskell98
# roadmap's D37 was for share/rhc/haskell98). The ground is a correction of the Report's text (corrections.tsv), one of
# the roadmap's readings of 2010's text (N1 to N21) or decisions (D1 to D41), a section of the 2010 Report, or, written
# 98:X, the haskell98 roadmap's X (a decision, a reading R1 to R54, a ruling) or 98's entry of the same id
# (share/rhc/haskell98/overlay.tsv): the Prelude's code is 98's but for four lines of imports, and Data.Array,
# Data.Complex and Data.Ratio continue 98's Array, Complex and Ratio, so 98's entries on them carry where the code
# does, with what 2010 changes said. The modules of this directory are the code as printed (pristine/) with the entries
# marked applied. An entry marked listed is decided and not yet written; open is a choice not taken; none is a place
# where the text and the code disagree and the code stands. A module, or a line of one, that no applied entry names is
# the Report's, token for token (hs2010/library/overlay). The modules the Report prints no code for are no entries
# here: provenance.tsv says where each one's code comes from (D23, D24).
# Columns: id; module (each one the entry touches); where (the definitions, in Haskell's words); lines (in pristine/,
# which never changes); kind; ground; status (applied, listed, open, none); change.
# Kinds: erratum (a correction changes the code: one of 98's errata read into 2010's text where it is 98's, D38 (a)
# (i)); reading (the code departs from the Report's own text, or a misprint); unresolved (names that do not resolve as
# printed); builtin (declared "Not legal Haskell; for illustration only"); elided (the Report writes ... for a body or
# a type); primitive (a prim name, a module the Report never defines, or a signature with no binding); instances
# (given by a scheme: "similar", "as derived"); representation (the same meaning by other means); option (may be

column8: change

As 98's: PreludeBuiltin and UnicodePrims, which the Report imports and never defines, are rhc's runtime in Core (CoreRuntime), no files of the library, hidden from programs; PreludeRuntime, rhc's module of Core's primitives and what the library builds on them in Haskell, hidden, in the Prelude's unit, is the runtime layer both libraries share (D25's B), and PreludeRuntime2010 the part of it that 2010's library alone has.
seq = primSeq, the runtime's (CoreRuntime).

Built-in syntax: the type and its constructor are rhc's, with the instances its deriving clause names (Eq, Ord, Enum, Bounded), as chapter 11 derives them; Show and Read are PreludeText's, Ix is Data.Ix's.
Built-in syntax: the type and its constructors are rhc's, with Eq and Ord as derived.

Built-in syntax: the types and their constructors are rhc's, with Eq, Ord and Bounded written as chapter 11 derives them, for every size (ov.tuples.fifteen), and lexOrder, the order of their components.

column3: data Char; instance Enum Char; instance Bounded Char
column8: A Char is a code point in a Mid int, 0 to 0x10FFFF, surrogates among them; primIntToChar, primCharToInt and primUnicodeMaxChar are rhc's primitives, and maxBound is '\x10FFFF'.

column3: data IO a; instance Monad IO: (>>=), return
column8: IO passes a state token: data IO a is rhc's primitive type, and (>>=) and return are the runtime's primBindIO and primReturnIO.

column3: data Int, and its instances Eq, Ord, Num, Real, Integral, Enum, Bounded
column8: As 98's: Int is Mid's int, 63 bits, its instances over int_*, maxBound 2^62 - 1 and minBound -2^62, Enum Int bounded (98:R40). Its arithmetic is 98's checked one, an overflow an error, until M11 makes it wrap modulo 2^63 in both modes over Rune's wrapping int primitives (D21's C with B2), and this entry with 98's says so.

column3: data Integer, and its instances Eq, Ord, Num, Real, Integral, Enum
column8: Integer has IntInf's representation, the instances over integer_*; the enumFrom family strict in all its arguments (6.3.4).

column3: data Float, and its instances Eq, Ord, Num, Real, Fractional, Floating, RealFrac, RealFloat
column8: As 98's: a Float is a Double that binary32 represents, each result rounded to binary32, the instances over float_*; fromRational by Numeric's fromRat, which the Prelude imports.

column3: data Double, and its instances Eq, Ord, Num, Real, Fractional, Floating, RealFrac, RealFloat
column8: As 98's: a Double is Mid's real, a binary64, the instances over double_*; fromRational is Numeric's fromRat (the Prelude imports it).

column3: instance Enum Float; instance Enum Double: enumFrom, enumFromThen
column8: 98's erratum, read into 2010's text, which is 98's here word for word and lacks it (D38 (a)(i), N18): enumFrom x = x `seq` numericEnumFrom x and enumFromThen x y = x `seq` y `seq` numericEnumFromThen x y, so that the code is strict in all its arguments as 6.3.4 says; numericEnumFrom and numericEnumFromThen stay as printed, and Data.Ratio's Enum, which shares them, is not made strict.

Data.Ratio's Enum names the four, which the Prelude defines and does not export (Data.Ratio's comment: "but not exported from it!"): their lines are PreludeEnum's, a module of the runtime layer both libraries share (D25), hidden from programs, which the Prelude and Data.Ratio import.

primError is the runtime's (CoreRuntime): an exception of the kind ErrorCall, which catch does not see (3.1, 7.3); a program that ends in one ends as 98's chapter 23 says, its text on the standard error and status 1 (D38 (d)(i): implementation-defined, as 98's).

column3: the tuples of 4 to 15 components, and every tuple's instances the code does not give
column8: Every implementation supports tuples up to size 15, with Eq, Ord, Bounded, Read and Show (6.1.4). The code gives Eq, Ord and Bounded for pairs and triples, and Show and Read for pairs, and says the rest are "similar": they are written by the same scheme, sizes 2 to 15, as 98's are. Data.Ix's, to 15 too (N16, D38 (c)), are Data.Ix's own code (provenance.tsv).

words qualifies isSpace by Char, Char.isSpace, where the import is now import qualified Data.Char(isSpace) (the sources' f08a901 renamed 98's import, not its uses), and a qualified name's qualifier is the module's name or its alias: both uses are Data.Char.isSpace. GHC 9.4.7 -XHaskell2010: "Not in scope: `Char.isSpace'". Not among the roadmap's defects of the text.

98's erratum, read into 2010's text, which is 98's here word for word and lacks it (D38 (a)(i), N18): the third guard is isIdInit c, the underscore is out of isSingle's list, and isIdInit c = isAlpha c || c == '_' is a local definition, so that lex reads an identifier with a leading underscore as one lexeme, as 2.4 says. The lexer's other limits stand, as its comment says (98:R43).

column3: instance Show Float; instance Show Double
column8: showsPrec p = showSigned showFloat p: a negative number parenthesised above precedence 6, as Show Integer's showSigned showInt is, against the printed showsPrec p = showFloat, which drops p (11.4: enclosed in parentheses where the precedence is less than d, and syntactically correct). 98's ruling R42; 2010's chapters 9 and 11 are 98's here.
As ov.prelude.imports; PreludeIO imports IOError's details from PreludeRuntime, and its readFile, writeFile and appendFile in place of the runtime's (ov.preludeio.prims).

column3: data IOError; instance Show IOError; instance Eq IOError
column8: data IOError stands as printed, rhc's primitive type: Core's Exn of the kind IOError, the exception catch sees. Its details are PreludeRuntime's, over Core's: its kind, its text, its file and its handle. Show IOError gives the text, or user error (TEXT) for a user's; Eq compares all four.

column3: ioError, userError, catch, putChar, getChar, getContents, readFile, writeFile, appendFile
column8: As 98's: the nine prim names are the runtime's (CoreRuntime), readFile's, writeFile's and appendFile's PreludeRuntime's, which PreludeIO imports in their place, under the locks a file is held by; getChar and getContents read the standard input through one buffer, which System.IO's hGetChar stdin and hGetLine stdin share; readFile and getContents read lazily, a chunk at a time; input and output are UTF-8; catch sees an IOError and nothing else.

getLine = hGetLine stdin, as 7.1 says ("reads a line of text"), as 98's: the end of the file ends a line that has a character (the printed loop of getChar raises and loses it). PreludeIO imports hGetLine and stdin from PreludeRuntime2010, the runtime layer's 2010 part, where System.IO's handles of the standard input and output are, so that System.IO is not in the Prelude's unit (D23's cycle).

interact's body stands as printed: PreludeIO imports hSetBuffering, stdin, stdout and BufferMode from PreludeRuntime2010, which System.IO re-exports, not from System.IO, which would put it and Data.Ix in the Prelude's unit (D23's cycle: Prelude, PreludeList, PreludeText, PreludeIO, Data.Char, Numeric, Data.Ratio and the runtime layer, PreludeEnum, PreludeRuntime and PreludeRuntime2010).

The module is headed module  Array (, 98's name left in the chapter of module Data.Array, which exports module Data.Ix and is imported as Data.Array: it is module  Data.Array (. No source fix exists (the sources' Data-Array.tex:240 at every commit).

column3: data Array; array; (!); instance Functor (Array a)
column8: As 98's: an array is its bounds and an Arr of its elements, each at its index's place: (!) reads in constant time, where 14 has a programmer reasonably expect rapid access to the components. Each function means the Report's: array is strict in the indices (its inRange check, here 2010's guard) and not in the values; an element with no association, or with several, is an error where it is read, with 2010's texts; fmap is array over the elements. The rest of the module stands as printed.

array is strict in its bounds, as 14.2's prose says ("strict in the bounds argument and in the indices of the association list, but non-strict in the values", 98's sentence): array b ivs forces rangeSize b, so both bounds, before its guard, where the printed code checks the bounds only through inRange over the associations, so that array undefined [] is not bottom by the code. 98's ruling 35, the same text and the same code in this respect.

The import is dead, as 98's was: 2010's (//) needs no (\\). Dropping it takes Data.List and Data.Maybe out of Data.Array's closure; Data.Array is outside the Prelude's unit either way (D23). Not taken.

Data.Maybe defines maybe and exports it, where the Prelude, imported implicitly, defines and exports its own (9), so the export is ambiguous (5.5.2: "it must be possible unambiguously to resolve which entity is thereby referred to"); GHC 9.4.7: "Ambiguous occurrence". The definition goes and the export list's maybe is the Prelude's, as 98's Maybe re-exported it. Hiding the Prelude's maybe instead makes two entities of that name, so that every importer that names maybe unqualified is ambiguous. No source fix exists.

showsPrec p (x:%y) = showParen (p > ratPrec) showsPrec (ratPrec+1) x . ... y) is a parenthesis short and does not parse (GHC 9.4.7: "parse error on input `)'"): the line is 98's, (showsPrec (ratPrec+1) x . The sources lost it when 1dcaf12 turned the tabs of the lines into spaces; no source fix exists.
gcd's code and text agree, gcd 0 0 being an error. lcm's text says "the smallest positive integer that both x and y divide", where lcm _ 0 = 0: the code stands.
6.3.3 says every Prelude type but the function and IO types is an instance of Show and Read; the code gives IOError Show and Eq and no Read. No change.
The comment's 12 `reduce` (-8) == 3 :% (-2) holds of reduce, while (%) moves the sign first, as 22's text says; the message "Data.Ratio.% : zero denominator" stands.
